idiom_name: user-defined type guard over a per-element visitor interface
implementation_notes: instanceof narrows classes but not interfaces, so the acyclic test is normally written as a user-defined type guard - const isCircleVisitor = (v: Visitor): v is CircleVisitor => typeof (v as CircleVisitor).visitCircle === 'function' - and accept calls if (isCircleVisitor(visitor)) visitor.visitCircle(this);. Declared interfaces carry the per-element contract and the empty base interface carries the degenerate base, so the role structure exists in the type system without any emulation of multiple inheritance, and structural typing means a visitor object can satisfy an element-visitor interface without naming it. What replaces the classic double-dispatch Visitor in this language is the discriminated union with an exhaustiveness check (const exhausted: never = node), which is closed and therefore a different row; keep the guard-based visitor when element types are added outside your package.
pitfalls: A type guard is a promise the compiler takes on faith: if the guard and the interface drift apart the narrowing is unsound, so keep them adjacent and cover the guard with a test of its own.
Interfaces are erased at runtime, so nothing enforces that a new element is handled by existing visitors - the same silent-skip failure as in Java, with no compiler backstop.
Declaring the per-element methods optional (visitCircle?) removes the need for the guard but lets name typos pass the type checker, turning the acyclic miss into a permanent bug.
